item.title: US envoy Witkoff to meet Putin, Trump presses Kyiv to settle
item.description: Zelenskiy told a news conference after the Oslo meeting that Ukraine was again receiving early warnings of Russian missile attacks.
item.dc:creator: Nerijus Adomaitis, Lina Golovnya, Steve Holland
item.content:encoded: US envoy Steve Witkoff will meet Russian President Vladimir Putin on Wednesday after what a US official called "constructive" talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy in Norway, as President Donald Trump said it was time for Ukraine to end the war. The US official said Ukraine brought forward new ideas and proposals to the Oslo talks, which also involved the leaders of Norway and Finland and European and NATO representatives, and that participants made "meaningful progress" toward a coordinated approach to engaging Russia. The official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, said the talks covered "key elements of a comprehensive peace framework," including security guarantees for Ukraine, a post-war economic plan and a broader European security architecture. Witkoff would aim to "create a pathway toward direct trilateral and broader multilateral negotiations," the official said. Zelenskiy travelled to Oslo seeking to repair relations with Washington, which have sunk to new lows as Trump has courted Moscow. Kyiv has complained that Washington has withheld vital military support and intelligence. Zelenskiy told a news conference after the Oslo meeting and an earlier phone call with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio that Ukraine was again receiving early warnings of Russian missile attacks. "Now it works, it's great," he said, adding he and Rubio had discussed supplies of Patriot missile interceptors as well as the satellite-based Starlink system, which Kyiv complained had stopped working when mounted on fast-moving objects such as drones. Trump's recent gestures toward Moscow, including a deal to buy Russian diesel and a waiver of new sanctions, sparked bipartisan pushback in the US Congress and worry in European capitals. Zelenskiy said he had discussed "Article 5-like" security guarantees, referring to the NATO stipulation that an attack on one ally is an attack on all. "I am thankful to the American side that they underlined again that it will be strong," he said. Zelenskiy reiterated that Ukraine hoped to discuss key issues on how to end the war during a trilateral meeting of leaders of Ukraine, Russia and the US. Norway's Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Stoere told the news conference the Oslo meeting had been good and constructive, while Finnish President Alexander Stubb added: "I think the (peace) process is back on track." Washington has denied deliberately hindering Ukraine's war effort. But Trump has repeatedly [USN:L6N4611D3 TEXT:"rebuked Zelenskiy"], and called for him to be [USN:L6N45W06G TEXT:"replaced"]. On Tuesday, Trump called on Ukraine to make a deal to settle the war, and said Moscow wanted to get it done. "Ukraine has to want to settle this war," he told reporters. Trump suggested Moscow had the upper hand in the fight because "Russia is a big machine — they just keep grinding forward, and that's what they've done. They've taken a very large piece of land." RUBIO SAYS US MISSILES MAY NOT HAVE BEEN DELIVERED YET The US under Trump has largely stopped providing weapons directly to Ukraine but lets European countries buy US weaponry on Kyiv's behalf under a program known as Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List (PURL). It has also provided intelligence and technology that Europe cannot match. A source familiar with the matter said most weapons deliveries under PURL continued to flow, but US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth had not approved Ukraine’s latest requests for Patriot interceptors. Rubio acknowledged on Tuesday that a consignment of interceptors bought by European countries for Ukraine may not have been delivered, but denied that the US had changed policy. "There has not been some deliberate political directive to go out and harm Ukraine," he said on a visit to India. Hegseth told reporters US policy toward Ukraine had not changed and stressed the need to maintain US stockpiles. "Certainly, with things like interceptors, we want to make sure our guys have the most possible as well," he said. He also said Washington had [USN:SPN4650B4 TEXT:"not pulled back Ukraine's ability to access Starlink"], which is owned by Elon Musk's SpaceX, and appeared to signal that the problem rested with corporate terms of service Kyiv needed to comply with. Musk has said Starshield, the military-grade version of SpaceX's Starlink communications system, is controlled by the US government and any limits on its use are ultimately up to Trump. Tuesday's Wall Street Journal cited US officials and people familiar with the matter as saying that Musk ordered the slowdown after consulting with Trump and other administration officials. Reuters [USN:L1N4610ZC TEXT:"reported"] earlier that the order to limit the service came from the White House. While US ties with Ukraine have deteriorated, Russia has stepped up attacks on Ukrainian cities, particularly targeting power stations and fuel, despite a call from Trump for both sides to spare each other's energy systems. Russia bombarded cities in western Ukraine overnight, targeting electricity systems and [USN:L1N4660DM TEXT:"knocking out power"] across swathes of the country that had previously been spared. Ukraine held back for several days last week from hitting Russian oil refineries in deference to Trump's request, but has resumed strikes after Russia showed no sign of complying. Both sides have also struck data centres. Trump has repeatedly condemned Ukrainian attacks on Russia while saying little about Russia's far more severe attacks on Ukraine. RUSSIAN ATTACKS Russia's defence ministry said on Tuesday it struck three cargo vessels in Ukraine's port of Reni and two other cargo vessels en route to Odesa. Russian forces also hit two logistics hubs, it said. Energy facilities were attacked in seven Ukrainian regions overnight, knocking out power, and the western Lviv region was struck again during the day. Russian drones also struck an energy facility in Kyiv on Tuesday, mayor Vitali Klitschko said, with authorities saying power was out in four districts. The deterioration of US-Ukraine relations began 10 days ago when Trump lifted sanctions on Russian diesel in a deal agreed with Putin. Trump said this would help reduce high fuel prices that have upset US voters ahead of midterm elections on November 3. At the weekend, Trump issued a broad waiver of tougher sanctions on Russia that were meant to have begun this week.

item.title: Takeaways: Key findings from our investigation of supersized heat waves
item.description: Reuters conducted a data-driven examination of global temperatures.
item.dc:creator: Maurice Tamman
item.content:encoded: Heat waves have evolved from sporadic, isolated episodes to massive, cascading weather events that blanket vast swaths of the planet for months or even years at a time. To continue calling such sprawling phenomena “heat waves” would be like calling a monsoon a rain shower. To understand the new reality of these immense expanses of heat, Reuters consulted with two dozen climate researchers and analyzed temperatures around the globe for every hour of every day since 1960. From those results, we developed a new concept: the “heat storm.” Scientists and researchers often discuss global warming in the context of risks that will arise if the planet’s average global temperature rises more than 2°C (3.6°F) above pre-industrial levels. What is an ordinary person to make of that? Not much. Heat waves are the connective tissue between the science of global warming and our everyday experience. But supersized heat waves used to be rare. No longer. Now they swarm the planet. Naming events is “a powerful way for people to understand that something is happening,” Anthony Leiserowitz, director of the Yale Program on Climate Change Communication, told Reuters. Yet “we don't currently do that with heat waves,” he said, even though heat has been estimated to kill almost half a million people a year. Read more at https://www.reuters.com/investigates/special-report/climate-heatstorms-takeaways/

item.title: As France erupts, Europe's far right gains from fuel-price anger ahead of elections
item.description: Cost-of-living pressures are driving unrest and giving fresh momentum to far-right parties ahead of next year's elections in France, Italy and Poland.
item.dc:creator: Michel Rose, Angelo Amante, Miranda Murray
item.content:encoded: The tractors rolling into the town of Gela on the southern tip of Europe are flying the Sicilian flag, emblazoned with Medusa, three bent legs and ears of wheat, a reminder of the island's role as a breadbasket since Roman times. But the farmers are not bringing in a harvest. They are protesting. As soaring fuel prices squeeze household budgets and businesses across Europe, cost-of-living pressures are driving unrest and giving fresh momentum to far-right parties ahead of elections next year in countries including France, Italy and Poland. Parties once considered fringe had already been gaining ground, with voters from motorists in rural France to young men in Germany's former Communist east looking for alternatives. The US-Iran war , which erupted in February and sent energy prices sharply higher, has compounded the challenge for governments already struggling to contain inflation, support growth and rein in spending. The discontent has spilled onto the streets. In France, demonstrations that began over deteriorating school facilities in Paris' northern suburbs have morphed into some of the country's worst unrest in decades, with shops looted, buildings torched and a 19th-century town hall in Limoges set on fire. "Why am I here? Well, quite simply, I find the current cost of living truly terrifying," said Quentin Leviloux, a 21-year-old protester in Nantes. "Just think of people who earn barely the minimum wage, when you look at the cost of food, fuel, and everything else. It’s terrifying how incredibly expensive things have become." The European Commission estimates the Iran conflict has cost Europe roughly €100 billion ($112 billion) through disrupted trade and energy markets. Gas prices have jumped about 140% and diesel prices have doubled. In a weekend address, French President Emmanuel Macron acknowledged the "legitimate demands" of protesters angered by rising living and fuel costs, while condemning those responsible for violence and looting. "We must never confuse them with those who destroyed, vandalised and looted," he said. PROTESTS ERUPT ACROSS EUROPE Violence has also erupted elsewhere. In the wealthy northern Italian city of Milan, police clashed on Sunday with protesters hurling stones and [USN:L8N4650S6 TEXT:"looting stores"] during demonstrations over poor public services and rising living costs. In Gela, on Sicily's southern coast, farmers say fuel costs have made operating machinery prohibitively expensive. "We cultivate the land, we harvest debts," said one banner. "We are completely at a standstill," said Arcangelo Gambino, a farmers' representative in Caltanissetta province. "The (fuel) cost has more than doubled." Roadblocks by truckers, farmers and steelworkers have disrupted transport across parts of southern Italy, contributing to local fuel shortages and concerns over supermarket supplies. Tens of thousands [USN:L8N46304H TEXT:"marched through Lisbon"] on Saturday over low wages, housing costs and the rising cost of living, increasing pressure on Portugal's centre-right government. In Spain, the eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her home [USN:L1N45U0F8 TEXT:"sparked nationwide demonstrations"] over housing shortages and soaring rents, helping trigger a snap election next month. Belgium has also seen demonstrations, while [USN:L6N464038 TEXT:"large rallies in Albania"] have been driven by anger over perceived government corruption, a lack of jobs and poor education standards. The protests reflect broader economic anxieties that are increasingly shaping politics across the continent. Concerns about purchasing power have become "a major driver of populist politics" across Europe, said Gilles Ivaldi, a political scientist at Sciences Po. Politicians on both the hard right and hard left have increasingly argued that restoring energy ties with Russia would help lower costs, challenging Europe's mainstream consensus on support for Ukraine. LE PEN MAKES FUEL PRICES A CAMPAIGN ISSUE The latest energy shock comes after years of economic strain following the pandemic and the fallout from Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine. In France, rising energy costs have provided an explosive backdrop to next April's presidential election. Macron's government is struggling with a ballooning budget deficit and pressure from bond markets. Frontrunner Marine Le Pen of the far-right National Rally and hard-left veteran Jean-Luc Melenchon have both made fuel prices central planks in their campaigns. “Rising fuel prices are clearly an issue that boosts Marine Le Pen,” said Ivaldi. “I think this is an issue she has owned for quite some time." Since the Iran war began, [USN:L8N43B0GJ TEXT:"Le Pen's ratings"] have improved while Macron's have slipped, according to polling by Elabe. Le Pen's [USN:L1N45S0C4 TEXT:"proposal to sharply cut"] value-added tax on fuel has attracted broad public support. Analysts say the issue resonates strongly with her core voters in rural and semi-rural areas where car travel is often essential. CALLS TO RESTORE RUSSIA TIES In neighbouring Germany, the Alternative for Germany (AfD) is leading national opinion polls after [USN:L1N45C01D TEXT:"strong gains in local elections"]. The cost of living topped Germans' concerns for a fifth straight year in a survey published this month. [USN:L8N45M0FI TEXT:"German inflation spiked"] to nearly a three-year high in September, with energy price inflation rising to 14.9%, handing ammunition to the AfD to [USN:L6N45D0RG TEXT:"attack Chancellor Friedrich Merz"]. The AfD is pushing to [USN:L8N4591QO TEXT:"restore energy ties"] with Russia, arguing that Berlin’s support for Ukraine is needlessly self-sabotaging at a time when Europe’s largest economy and many of its energy-hungry companies are struggling. Past experience indicates a link between high energy prices and voter turnout for the AfD, said Jan Steckel, professor for the political economy of climate change at the Technical University of Munich. “Populist parties often frame energy costs as avoidable and attribute them to government policy choices ... rather than to the underlying geopolitical shocks that drive them," he said. “These geopolitical shocks are ... much more difficult to explain. And I think this is why incumbent parties often struggle." The argument is gaining traction elsewhere. In Italy, Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni faces growing competition from National Future, a new far-right party led by former army general Roberto Vannacci that advocates restoring gas links with Russia. In Poland, one of Ukraine's staunchest supporters, concern over energy bills is helping boost support for the far-right Confederation of the Polish Crown. Its leader, Grzegorz Braun, has called for a return to buying Russian oil and gas, making the case alongside AfD politicians in Lubmin, where the damaged Nord Stream pipelines land in Germany. “I love the smell of Russian gas in the morning,” he said. ($1 = 0.8921 euros)

item.title: Sudanese drone attack killed more than 150 people in Abyei market, official says
item.description: South Sudanese officials said Sudan's military had carried out drone strikes that hit a market in the disputed Abyei region, killing more than 150 people, the latest in a series of strikes in one of the bloodiest weeks of a war that has spilled across Sudan's borders.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: South Sudanese officials said Sudan's military had carried out drone strikes that hit a market in the disputed Abyei region, killing more than 150 people, the latest in a series of strikes in one of the bloodiest weeks of a war that has spilled across Sudan's borders. The strike pushed the toll from attacks in recent days to more than 250, underscoring the lethality of airstrikes in [USN:L6N40Y0KB TEXT:"Sudan's war"], which erupted in April 2023 between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), triggering a major humanitarian crisis and drawing in local militias and foreign powers. Yohana Akol Ngor, the caretaker minister of information in Abyei, told Reuters on Tuesday that the death toll from the attack on the market in Abyei on Monday had jumped to 153 from 73, but was likely to rise further. "The fire is still burning. So the recovery process of the dead ones is still continuing. The situation is terrible," Ngor said, adding that some bodies had been burned to ashes. A video filmed at the scene on Tuesday and verified by Reuters showed the charred and twisted remains of vehicles and buildings. Flames still billowed from one building as residents inspected the damage. He said Sudan's army was responsible for the attack, without providing evidence. A spokesperson for Sudan's armed forces did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Three diplomatic sources, an aid worker and an expert on the conflict told Reuters the strike hit a fuel depot in the market. The diplomatic sources said the depot had been used in the past by the RSF to supply its forces. A spokesperson for the RSF did not immediately respond to requests for comment. OIL-RICH ABYEI South Sudan declared independence from Sudan in 2011. Since then, both countries have staked a claim to oil-rich Abyei, which is jointly administered. It borders Sudan's Kordofan region, which has become a major centre of fighting in the war. Officials in Sudan's military-led government told Reuters the RSF is active in parts of Abyei. Ngor denied the presence of the RSF in Abyei. Reuters could not immediately verify the claims. The United Nations Interim Security Force for Abyei (UNISFA) warned in May that the presence of the RSF in Abyei had increased insecurity there, adding that delays in determining the disputed region's final status had put civilians and UNISFA personnel at risk. UN spokesperson Stephane Dujarric said the UN strongly condemned the series of drone attacks in Abyei and other areas. "We remain alarmed by the relentless drone attacks across Sudan, as well as the damage they are causing to critical infrastructure - these attacks are taking a devastating toll on communities already struggling with the consequences of more than three years of conflict," Dujarric told reporters in New York. STRUGGLE TO RETRIEVE BODIES Ngor told Reuters that emergency workers had struggled to retrieve the bodies because of fires caused by the strikes. Some 8,000 people had been displaced by Monday's bombing, Ngor added. South Sudan's foreign ministry said late on Monday that drones struck a market located north of Abyei town, but did not specify the number of civilian casualties or provide a toll. The ministry said it had summoned the Sudanese ambassador in protest. An eyewitness said he heard five large explosions that led to the fuel market catching fire. "People started evacuating the casualties. They had injuries from shrapnel on their stomach and legs ... In one site, I saw 28 bodies that were burnt," the witness said, asking not to be named for safety reasons. The witness said they did not see any sign of RSF or other uniformed fighters in the market, where goods like sugar, flour and biscuits are also sold for shipment into Sudan. DEADLY WEEK Sudanese armed forces and the RSF have recently escalated [USN:L6N44V0K3 TEXT:"drone strikes"], with a series of attacks targeting RSF-held Nyala and army-held Khartoum airport this week. On Sunday, drone attacks in West Kordofan state in Sudan, controlled by the RSF, killed some 84 people and injured 65 others, according to the local Emergency Response Room. On Monday, four children were killed after repeated drone attacks targeted SAF-controlled Khartoum airport. On Friday, an attack on a market in RSF stronghold Nyala killed 23 people and injured 44, according to volunteers there. Chadian authorities have accused Sudan’s military of carrying out drone strikes on its territory, which UN experts say is regularly used by RSF supply lines. Sudan's foreign ministry said in late August that its armed forces were acting to protect the country's security. On October 10, [USN:L1N45X06E TEXT:"an airstrike"] close to Sudan's border with Egypt killed more than 70 artisanal miners, according to a local rights group. PATIENTS TREATED FOR BURNS Abyei experiences frequent bouts of violence, with clashes usually involving rival ethnic groups or armed militias. The attack is the deadliest in years to hit the area, where medical supplies and healthcare are scarce. South Sudan's government says it has not taken sides in its neighbour's war. However, diplomats and experts say Abyei has established itself as crucial, serving as a transit point for RSF logistics, particularly fuel. Medical charity Medecins Sans Frontieres (MSF) said it was treating more than 20 wounded, some with burns, at the nearby Ameth Bek Hospital. "We are providing surgical services and wound dressing, along with other emergency care," said Christian Lindauer, MSF medical activities manager at the facility. Photographs shared on MSF's official social media account showed bandaged patients lying on the floor as they received care for their injuries.

item.title: France to deploy troops, admits to failures over weekend unrest
item.description: The turmoil shocked France because of both its scale and the apparent inability of police to contain it, inflaming tensions ahead of presidential elections next year.
item.dc:creator: Elizabeth Pineau, Dominique Vidalon
item.content:encoded: France will reinforce police with troops and mount a huge security operation for more protests planned on Saturday, the government said on Tuesday, acknowledging failures in its response to [USN:L1N46401W TEXT:"last weekend's violence"]. "The deployment next Saturday will be massive," Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said, adding that the immediate priority was to restore order after rioting and looting swept Paris, Marseille, Lyon and other cities on October 17. In a sometimes rowdy debate, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said the military would be deployed alongside police, while the government pledged to overhaul tactics after widespread criticism that city centres had been left vulnerable. TARGETED CURFEWS HELP RESTORE CALM Framing the crisis as a choice "between violence and the Republic", Lecornu blamed the unrest on far-left groups, who in turn have accused the government of underestimating [USN:L1N4650EF TEXT:"public anger"] over high living costs and declining public services. The turmoil shocked France because of both its scale and the apparent inability of police to contain it, inflaming tensions ahead of presidential elections next year with candidates from the far right and hard left performing strongly in polls. Protests in other European countries, including [USN:L8N4650S6 TEXT:"Italy"] and [USN:L6N464038 TEXT:"Albania"], have added to concerns that anger over living standards risks spreading around the continent at a time when many nations, including France, are struggling with budget woes. A night of relative calm in France followed [USN:L6N4650BY TEXT:"targeted curfews"] imposed in several areas affected by the chaos, which the government said had helped reassert control. The localised curfews, some directed at children and teenagers under age 18, were extended to Tuesday night, police said. Lecornu acknowledged shortcomings in the state's response at the weekend, saying there had been intelligence failures, while police deployments had been too static and authorities had erred by not cancelling planned police leave. Nunez apologised for the mistakes. "I deeply regret what happened. I accept my share of responsibility," he said. SUSPECT ARRESTED FOR LIMOGES TOWN HALL DESTRUCTION Parliament is setting up a commission of inquiry to establish the causes of the unrest, while authorities have assigned 200 investigators to identify and track down those involved in the street violence. Police arrested on Tuesday a man suspected of starting a blaze that destroyed a historic town hall in the central city of Limoges during the rioting. Officials said he had been on a security watch list and belonged to an ultra-left group. Sylvain Maillard, a Renaissance deputy for Paris, told Reuters some apps had become "a walkie-talkie system for rioters and looters". Underscoring the broad impact of the crisis, French borrowing costs rose further on Tuesday as investors fretted about the prospect of more unrest, with the yield on benchmark 10-year government bonds touching its highest level in 24 years. Supermarket chain Carrefour said it had lost tens of millions of euros through [USN:L6N46612N TEXT:"theft and damage"], warning that it faced an "unprecedented situation" because of the disorder. France's main student union UNEF has called for further protests on Saturday, pledging to maintain pressure on Macron's government over what it says is a deteriorating and underfunded education system. "We carry on," it said on social media. Separately, groups identifying themselves as "Gilets Jaunes" (Yellow Vests) called for protest actions over rising fuel costs. The yellow vest movement, largely inactive in recent years, sprang up in 2018 during Macron's first term over plans to raise petrol taxes. Traffic blockades continued for months until the government made costly concessions it can ill afford now. ITALY FACES NEW FORM OF UNREST, MINISTER SAYS Northern Italian cities, including the financial capital Milan, were also hit by riots last weekend. Though not on the scale seen in France, the unrest nonetheless jolted Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni's government, which was expected to introduce new security measures at a cabinet meeting on Tuesday. Defence Minister Guido Crosetto described the disturbances as a form of "hybrid warfare" conducted through social media platforms such as TikTok, YouTube and other online networks. "The events in Milan and elsewhere in Italy are fundamentally different from those seen in other eras," Crosetto wrote on X. "The West has yet to realise this or take any meaningful action in response." In Milan's central Corso Vittorio Emanuele II, sportswear retailer On and a Levi's store that were targeted during the unrest had reopened on Tuesday but remained boarded up. Luxury stores had restored merchandise to window displays after temporarily removing it for security reasons. In Albania, protesters were expected to take to the streets of Tirana for a seventh consecutive day against the government of Prime Minister Edi Rama.

item.title: France in turmoil: What might follow a weekend of riots?
item.description: France is counting the cost of some of its worst unrest in years at the weekend over the cost of living and under-funded public services. Here is the latest:
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: France is counting the cost of some of its [USN:L1N46401W TEXT:"worst unrest in years"] at the weekend over the cost of living and under-funded public services. Here is the latest: HOW WILL THE GOVERNMENT STOP MORE VIOLENCE AND HELP VICTIMS? Authorities say 2,500 people are in custody awaiting questioning while 149 are detained awaiting trial. [USN:L8N4650PE TEXT:"Partial curfews"] have been imposed in parts of Paris, Bordeaux, Lille, Lyon, Nice and Marseille to keep the streets quiet in areas worst-hit by rioting. The government, which had 60,000 officers mobilised at the weekend, plans to increase police numbers on the ground. For businesses and victims of violence, the government is implementing state-financed furlough measures to avoid layoffs, and providing funds to help companies meet cashflow needs. Insurers have promised speedy payouts to cover some of the damage, which hit more than 3,000 shops. HOW WILL THE GOVERNMENT ADDRESS UNDERLYING COMPLAINTS? France's extremely strained public finances mean the government has precious little room for broader measures to address protesters' anger over the rising cost of living. It has already hiked emergency spending this year to help certain sectors like farmers, fishermen and haulers cope with high fuel costs caused by the Iran war . The protests [USN:L1N45S0C7 TEXT:"began last month at high schools"] in Paris' working-class northern suburbs, where anger over teacher shortages and shabby facilities evolved into a broader movement. The government has so far not committed to substantial extra funding for schools but [USN:L6N45V0FM TEXT:"has pledged"] to send some 3,000 teachers, who are qualified but not yet working, to fill staffing gaps. HAVE PROTESTS PEAKED? Cities [USN:L6N4660DJ TEXT:"were quieter"] at the start of the week. But some protesters have called for a new round of demonstrations on Saturday. Unions have called for strikes on November 5 to protest budget cuts and support hiking wages. Schools are on a break for two weeks, but some student organisations are calling for more demonstrations. HOW WILL FRANCE'S DIRE ECONOMIC SITUATION BE AFFECTED? The unrest is a blow to business confidence, which was already fragile due to a fiscal crisis and high energy prices. The minority government is struggling to pass spending cuts in a divided parliament as part of its 2027 budget and is at risk of being toppled by opposition parties if a compromise cannot be found with at least some of them. The government wants to cut its budget deficit to 5.0% of economic output next year from 5.4% this year – one of the biggest in the euro zone. French bond yields [USN:L6N4660NP TEXT:"climbed further"] on Tuesday after their biggest daily rise in nearly a month in the previous session, with investors remaining cautious. The yield on France's 10-year benchmark bond reached 4.96% at one point on Tuesday. WILL THE UNREST SPREAD TO OTHER COUNTRIES? If France cannot contain the unrest, there is a risk that it could [USN:L8N4611KF TEXT:"spill across its borders"] with deep public anger around Europe over cost-of-living issues. In neighbouring Italy, [USN:L8N46407Z TEXT:"clashes erupted"] between police and protesters on Sunday. Albania has also seen a series of student demonstrations in recent days over corruption, a lack of jobs and poor education standards, while Spain and Portugal have faced protests over housing. HOW WILL THE UNREST AFFECT THE 2027 PRESIDENTIAL ELECTION? Elections next year will see President Emmanuel Macron step down after a decade in power. The unrest is likely to boost far-right presidential candidate Marine Le Pen, who is already the frontrunner in polls and has long talked tough on law and order. "Le Pen no longer needs to spend any money to campaign," Jean-Baptiste Moreau, a former lawmaker from Macron's camp, [USN:L6N4650JF TEXT:"told Reuters"]. "It's not just a clear path ahead of her, it's a six-lane highway." Hard-left candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon has come under pressure for backing protesters' demands, criticising the government's handling and not clearly condemning the violence. Meanwhile, Macron, who headed off to the Middle East on Monday, has emerged from the crisis further weakened. His former Prime Minister Edouard Philippe, now a centre-right presidential candidate, said on X he wanted "decisions and initiatives" from the lame-duck leader to "restore order". ARE PARIS AND OTHER CITIES SAFE TO VISIT? There have been no reports of any injuries to foreigners caught up in the unrest. However, several European governments [USN:L8N4650JR TEXT:"advised citizens"] travelling to France to avoid large crowds and exercise caution.

item.title: Dodge the cops, reach the protest: India's latest online political game goes viral
item.description: A web-based multiplayer game in which players dodge police and detention on their way to a protest site in New Delhi has gone viral, as young Indians use satire and humour to respond to police actions.
item.dc:creator: Tora Agarwala, Aftab Ahmed
item.content:encoded: A web-based multiplayer game in which players dodge police and detention on their way to a protest site in New Delhi has gone viral, as young Indians use satire and humour to respond to police actions. As [USN:L6N46206J TEXT:"youth-led protests"] over [USN:L4N3TC0XX TEXT:"jobs"], [USN:L4N43O0C9 TEXT:"exam paper leaks"] and [USN:L4N45K0E7 TEXT:"voter roll revisions"] spread across India, a growing crop of online games is transforming political grievances into shareable digital content. The trend shows a generation raised on Instagram is expressing dissent in ways that differ sharply from the political communication style of Prime Minister Narendra Modi. One such game, 'Jantar Mantar Chalo', was developed by 27-year-old IT professional Suraj Kushwah, who has described it as "dark humour". The game satirises the difficulties protesters face in reaching Jantar Mantar, a main protest site in the capital, amid police blockades, road closures and public transport suspensions. Players can build a kafila, or procession, evade checkpoints and stage a demonstration, or switch sides and deploy batons and tear gas to disperse crowds. "Whatever news was coming was kind of like a circus," Kushwah said. "People were trying to reach Jantar Mantar. And they were getting detained. And I imagined it as a 3D game." Kushwah said at least 2,000 people had been playing the game at any point in time since its release on October 14. Another game casts firebrand left-wing activist [USN:L4N45X011 TEXT:"Neha Bora"] as the protagonist of a retro 8-bit-style platform reminiscent of classic arcade games. "We as artists believe that satire is the most powerful way to talk about things," said 30-year-old Anav Nayar, who co-developed the game with his brother, Akshay. The protests were triggered by the "[USN:L1N43O05A TEXT:"cockroach""] youth movement, which also started as a joke online. The games draw inspiration from protests against the Election Commission's voter roll revision exercise, which opposition parties and activists say has disenfranchised 130 million eligible voters and favoured Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party. The Election Commission and BJP deny the allegations. Gen Z's style of expression poses an unusual challenge for Modi. After the "cockroach" movement forced the resignation of Modi's education minister in July, he intensified outreach to younger Indians through self-shot Instagram videos. But analysts say Modi's outreach might not be enough. "The BJP has long enough enjoyed its dominance of controlling the narrative online and on the ground, but this time the younger generation has countered them everywhere," said Rasheed Kidwai, a political analyst.

item.title: As Reliance Jio eyes listing, what are India's biggest share offerings?
item.description: Jio Platforms, the digital arm of billionaire Mukesh Ambani’s Reliance Industries , opened public bidding on Wednesday for its $3.2 billion IPO, India’s biggest and the first from the conglomerate in two decades.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Jio Platforms, the digital arm of billionaire Mukesh Ambani’s Reliance Industries (RELI.NS) , opened public bidding on Wednesday for its $3.2 billion IPO, India’s biggest and the first from the conglomerate in two decades. The company, whose businesses span telecoms, cloud computing, entertainment and AI services, is seeking a valuation of as much as $108.3 billion, with shares priced at 1,065 to 1,119 rupees each. Here are the five largest Indian IPOs to date: HYUNDAI MOTOR INDIA Hyundai (HYUN.NS) , the world's third-largest automaker and India's fourth-largest passenger vehicle maker, raised 278.7 billion rupees ($2.94 billion) in October 2024 in what is currently India's biggest-ever IPO. The manufacturer's South Korean parent (005380.KS) sold a 17.5% stake in a pure offer-for-sale, where existing shareholders sell shares and no new capital is raised. Jio Platforms is expected to use a similar approach, with the company's major investors set to dilute their stakes. NATIONAL STOCK EXCHANGE National Stock Exchange (NSEI.BO) became one of the world's 10 most valuable publicly traded bourses last month, with a market capitalisation of about $48 billion, after a [USN:L4N4590D5 TEXT:"$2.3 billion market debut"]. The stock listed at 1,800 rupees on the BSE on September 24, up 0.84% from its issue price of 1,785 rupees. LIFE INSURANCE CORPORATION OF INDIA The government pocketed roughly 205 billion rupees ($2.16 billion) from selling a 3.5% stake in India's largest insurer and biggest domestic financial investor (LIFI.NS) , a far cry from its initial target of up to $12 billion. The shares slid nearly 8% on their debut in May 2022. PAYTM [USN:L1N2S906S TEXT:"Paytm"] (PAYT.NS) , an Indian fintech firm, raised 183 billion rupees ($1.92 billion) in November 2021 in a mix of a fresh share issue and an offer for sale. Ant Group reduced its stake to 23% from 28% and SoftBank's Vision Fund cut its holding to 16%. Paytm lost more than 27% on its debut, the biggest listing-day drop in Indian IPO history at the time. TATA CAPITAL The Tata Group's financial services arm (TATC.NS) raised 155 billion rupees ($1.63 billion) in October 2025, with Tata Sons and IFC among those selling in the offer-for-sale component alongside a fresh issue. The IPO was the largest ever by a non-banking financial company in India. The shares [USN:L3N3VU09S TEXT:"listed"] at a slight premium of 1.23%. ($1 = 94.7800 Indian rupees)
